lines.text: Empire and papacy, painters and poets, a nation stitched together from many states. This is the long story of Italy, from Rome to the republic.
Tradition says Rome was founded on the Tiber in 753 BCE, a small settlement that would one day rule the Mediterranean.
The Romans threw out their kings and governed themselves through elected magistrates and a senate. The Republic won Italy, and then much more.
Its greatest test came when Hannibal of Carthage crossed the Alps and fought in Italy for years. Rome endured, and won the western Mediterranean.
Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon and made himself dictator, until senators struck him down on the Ides of March.
His heir Octavian won the civil wars that followed and, as Augustus, became the first Roman emperor, bringing a long peace.
The Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt, spreading roads, law and the Latin tongue.
In the year 79, Vesuvius erupted near Naples and buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving everyday Roman life under the ash.
In Rome, the Colosseum opened its gates to crowds watching gladiators and animal hunts. Much of it still stands.
Far to the north, people settled on islands in a lagoon. Their city of canals, Venice, would grow rich on trade.
In 476 a Germanic commander removed the last boy emperor of the West. Rome's empire in Italy was over.
Venice became a merchant republic under an elected doge, its ships linking Europe with the East for a thousand years.
In central Italy, the popes ruled their own lands as kings, the Papal States, with Rome at their heart.
In Bologna, students gathered to study law, founding what is seen as the oldest university in the Western world.
Francis of Assisi gave up his family's riches to live in poverty, founded the Franciscans, and became Italy's patron saint.
Thomas Aquinas, a friar from southern Italy, joined Aristotle's thought to Christian teaching and shaped the medieval Church.
From Venice, Marco Polo travelled all the way to the court of Kublai Khan, and his book opened European eyes to the East.
In Florence, Dante Alighieri was born, the poet who would choose Italian over Latin.
Florence began its great cathedral in 1296. More than a century later, Brunelleschi crowned it with a huge red brick dome.
Dante's Divine Comedy led readers through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, and made the Tuscan of Florence the base of the Italian language.
From the Italian cities came the Renaissance, a rebirth of classical learning and new ideas in art and science that spread across Europe.
In Florence, the Medici banking family took power, paying for artists like Donatello and Michelangelo, and giving the Church popes.
A sailor from Genoa, Christopher Columbus, sailed west for Spain in 1492 and reached the Caribbean, sure to the end it was Asia.
Leonardo da Vinci painted, engineered and studied the body and nature, filling notebooks with flying machines.
Amerigo Vespucci, a Florentine, sailed the coast of South America and wrote that it was a new continent. The Americas bear his name.
Niccolo Machiavelli, a Florentine diplomat, wrote The Prince, a frank account of how rulers really win and keep power.
Michelangelo carved the David and the Pieta, and painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
Raphael painted for the popes in Rome, and his School of Athens became a model of balance and grace. He died at only thirty-seven.
In Florence, Leonardo began a portrait of a woman with a faint smile. The Mona Lisa is now the most visited painting in the world.
In Rome, work began on a new St. Peter's Basilica. Bramante, Michelangelo and Bernini all left their mark, and Michelangelo's dome still rises over the city.
Galileo Galilei turned a telescope to the sky, saw the moons of Jupiter, and defended a Sun-centred universe. The Church condemned him.
Caravaggio painted saints as ordinary people in deep light and shadow, and lived a life as dramatic as his canvases.
In Venice, the priest and violinist Antonio Vivaldi wrote hundreds of concertos, The Four Seasons among them.
In 1800 Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs into the first chemical battery. The volt is named after him.
Giuseppe Garibaldi, a soldier who had fought in South America, came home to fight for a united Italy.
Giuseppe Verdi wrote Rigoletto, La traviata and Aida, music that Italians linked with their dream of unity.
After Napoleon's fall, the Risorgimento began: the long struggle to join the separate states of the peninsula into one Italy.
Giacomo Puccini was born in Tuscany. His operas, from La boheme to Tosca, are still among the most performed anywhere.
In 1860 Garibaldi landed in Sicily with about a thousand Red Shirts, took Sicily and Naples, and handed them to the king.
In 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed. A decade later, Rome became its capital.
Guglielmo Marconi made wireless telegraphy work, and in 1901 sent radio signals across the Atlantic.
Benito Mussolini, a journalist turned agitator, was born in 1883. He would lead Italy into dictatorship.
Enrico Fermi, a physicist from Rome, won a Nobel Prize, then left for America, where he built the first nuclear reactor.
After the First World War, Mussolini founded Fascism, a creed of extreme nationalism and one leader above all.
Federico Fellini, born in Rimini, would become one of the great film directors of the century.
In 1922 the Fascist squads marched on Rome, and the king made Mussolini prime minister. Dictatorship followed.
Allied with Hitler, Mussolini took Italy into the Second World War. It ended in defeat, and with Mussolini killed by partisans.
From the ruins came the Vespa, a cheap, stylish scooter that put postwar Italy back on the road.
In 1957, six countries signed the Treaty of Rome, founding the European Economic Community. Italy was among them.
Fellini's La Dolce Vita captured fame and parties in Rome, and gave the world the word paparazzi.
Giorgia Meloni was born in Rome. Decades later she would lead the Brothers of Italy to power.
Italy gave up the lira for the euro, a currency shared across much of the European Union.
After the global crash, a debt crisis shook southern Europe, and the future of the euro itself was debated.
In 2018 a motorway bridge in Genoa collapsed in a storm, killing forty-three people. A new bridge opened two years later.
In early 2020, Italy was among the first countries hit hard by COVID-19, and the nation went into lockdown.
And in 2026, Milan and Cortina shared the Winter Olympics, the first Games officially held by two cities.
From a village on the Tiber to a modern republic, Italy's past is never far beneath its streets.
